analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.15 an hour over two years.
analysis.headline: A one-member minimum wage bill was referred to a House committee in late October 2000, got no cosponsors, and died without ever reaching a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage from $5.15 an hour to $5.65 starting January 1, 2001, and to $6.15 starting January 1, 2002 — a $1 increase over two years [S2] [S3]. It was introduced in the final weeks of the 106th Congress by Rep. James Traficant of Ohio, referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never acted on further [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, most of them adults in retail, restaurants, and care work, would get a raise of up to $1 an hour — roughly $2,000 a year for a full-time worker at the proposed new floor.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 an hour for the year beginning January 1, 2001, and to $6.15 an hour beginning January 1, 2002 — a $1 increase over two years.
The increase applies through an amendment to the wage floor in section 6(a) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the law that sets the nationwide minimum wage for covered workers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay at or near the minimum wage — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service industries — bear the higher payroll, and some of the cost may be passed to consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers in retail and restaurants

drawbacks.text: The bill text as introduced contains a drafting gap: it states that $5.15 was in effect through June 30, 2000, but does not specify any wage amount for July 1 through December 31, 2000, leaving the wage floor for those months unclear.
A $1-an-hour wage floor raises labor costs for minimum-wage employers, and small businesses in low-wage sectors would face the same increase as large chains with no phase-in differences or offsets.
The bill includes no tax relief or other offsets for affected employers, unlike some competing minimum wage proposals debated in 2000 that paired the wage increase with business tax cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a full-time minimum-wage worker, the increase is worth roughly $2,000 a year, a substantial gain for the lowest-paid employees, while the cost falls on employers in the form of higher wages for their lowest-paid staff. The proposal is simple and direct but poorly drafted — it leaves the wage floor for the second half of 2000 unstated — and it arrived so late in the Congress, with no cosponsors, that it had no realistic path to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced October 25, 2000 and referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 without the bill ever getting a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. James Traficant of Ohio, the sole sponsor, introduced the Minimum Wage Act of 2000 on October 25, 2000, in the final weeks of the 106th Congress.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors [S4] and was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which has jurisdiction over the minimum wage.
On November 14, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay at or near the minimum wage are better off because the bill never moved: the federal floor stayed at $5.15 an hour, and the lowest-paid workers received no raise from this Congress.

for.name: Rep. James A. Traficant Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage by $1 over two years.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the minimum wage
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 25, 2000, and never reported the bill out or held a markup; it moved only to a subcommittee.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.role: House Education and the Workforce subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the referral from November 14, 2000 until the Congress ended without acting.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors of either party, so there is no roll-call record showing a partisan split; a minimum wage increase has generally divided along party lines, with Democrats supporting and Republicans opposing, a pattern widely reported during the 2000 wage debate.

industries.note: The industry employs more workers at or near the federal minimum wage than any other, so a $1-an-hour floor increase would raise its payroll directly; as the wage floor rises, its interest in holding it down runs against workers' paychecks.
Retail is a second major minimum-wage employer; the increase would raise wages for its lowest-paid staff, a cost the industry would resist or pass on through prices.

industries.industry: Other low-wage service employers (home care, cleaning, agriculture support services)
industries.note: Any employer paying between $5.15 and $6.15 would have to raise wages, which benefits their workers at their direct expense.
